title: LLM Integration with Existing Systems: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: LLM integration with existing systems connects a language model to a task inside software people already use. This guide explains how to choose that task, prepare its data, connect the model through your application, and test the result before a limited release. A fictional maintenance portal shows how the decisions fit together.

children.text: At a Glance

LLM integration with existing systems connects a language model to a task inside software people already use. This guide explains how to choose that task, prepare its data, connect the model through your application, and test the result before a limited release. A fictional maintenance portal shows how the decisions fit together.

Your team already uses an application to manage work. Staff still spend time reading long notes, rewriting information, or turning free-text requests into something another person can act on. A language model might help with part of that work, but adding an API call does not settle how the feature should behave.

You also need to decide which information the model can receive, who checks its output, and how people continue when it fails. Those decisions connect the proposed AI feature to the product you already operate.
What Is LLM Integration?

LLM integration connects a large language model to an application's data and workflow so users can complete a language-based task. The model might draft a summary, extract information from a document, classify a request, or help answer a question.

The application supplies the relevant input, sends a request to the model, and decides how to handle the response. Its existing business rules still determine who can access records, approve changes, and complete transactions.

A summary button on a request screen can be an LLM integration. You do not need to add a chatbot or let the model choose and perform actions independently. Those choices depend on what the user needs to accomplish.
Consider a
fictional maintenance-request portal

. A coordinator currently reads each request and its notes to prepare a handover summary. The proposed feature drafts the problem summary and identifies missing information. The coordinator checks that draft before using it. This example illustrates design decisions, not a real project or measured result.
How to Implement LLM Integration with Existing Systems

Start by defining the task and the information it requires. Then decide how the application will call the model, check its response, and present the result. Use the following steps to turn those decisions into an implementation that people can review.

The eight steps cover both development and the agreements around it. Resolve responsibilities and budget assumptions early, then revisit them as the data and application checks reveal the actual work.
Step 1: Choose One Task and Define a Useful Result

Choose a task with a clear beginning, an identifiable user, and an output that person can judge. “Add AI to our portal” leaves too many decisions open. “Draft a handover summary from this request's description and permitted notes” gives the feature a boundary.

Ask whether ordinary application logic could solve the problem first. A rule can route a request when its category already determines the destination. A language model may be worth testing when staff must interpret varied descriptions or condense free-text notes.
Use a short task definition to make the proposed result concrete:
Field
Portal Example
User
Coordinator preparing a handover
Current task
Read the request and notes, then write a summary
Input
Request description and relevant permitted notes
Output
Draft problem summary and missing-information list
Review
Coordinator compares the draft with the source
Exclusions
Dispatch, spending approval, and customer promises

Define usefulness against the current workflow. Does the draft preserve the reported problem? Does it omit an important note? Can the coordinator verify it without doing more work than writing the summary manually?
Write down examples of acceptable and unacceptable results before changing prompts. Anthropic's
evaluation guidance
recommends task-specific, measurable success criteria. Your criteria should reflect this task's consequences, rather than a generic claim that the model is accurate.
Step 2: Check What Your Existing System Can Provide

Review the parts of the application the feature must use before estimating the integration. The developer needs to understand where the relevant data lives, how users access it, and which application components can support the new behavior.

For the portal, inspect the request screen, the server-side code that retrieves its notes, and the rules that determine which coordinator may see them. Confirm access to a suitable development or test environment before using real records.
Record each item's status as
known
needs investigation
, or
not required
Check
What to Confirm
Application
Relevant code, APIs, and deployment access
Data
Fields, note sources, and permitted examples
Permissions
User roles and record access rules
Workflow
Current handover and review process

Missing documentation creates investigation work. An inaccessible data source may change the proposed scope. Neither situation supports a reliable estimate until someone checks what the application can actually provide.
The result of this step should be a small system map and a list of open questions. You need enough detail to identify the integration point, not a complete redesign of the product.
Step 3: Decide Which Data the Feature Needs

Give the model the information required for the selected task, with access rules applied before the request leaves your application. Separate data already available on the current record from information the feature would need to find elsewhere.

The portal's first version can use the request description and selected notes. It does not need every customer's history, unrelated requests, or staff account details. The application should select permitted fields and records for the current user.
Other features may need a different data path:
Data Need
Suitable Starting Point
Summarize the open request
Supply the permitted request content directly
Answer from a document collection
Retrieve relevant passages and include their sources
Use the current request status
Read the authoritative record through application logic
Retrieval-augmented generation, or
RAG
, adds retrieved information to the model's input. AWS's
retrieval documentation

illustrates the distinction between retrieving relevant source material and generating an answer from it. A feature that already has all its required text does not automatically need a separate retrieval system.

Decide how the feature handles incomplete or conflicting information. A recent note might correct the original report. Keep timestamps or note identifiers where they help staff trace the draft back to its source.

Review the selected provider's data handling and retention settings before sending company information. Agree which content may leave the application and what diagnostic logs may retain. Treat data copied into logs as part of that decision too.
Step 4: Connect the Model to Your Application

Put the model connection behind an application component that can enforce access rules, prepare the input, and check the response. For the portal, the coordinator requests a draft from the existing request screen, while server-side code handles the model API call.
An
LLM API integration
uses a provider's programmatic interface to send input and receive output. The portal's proposed request flow looks like this:
The coordinator selects
Draft Handover
on a request they may access.
The application checks permission and loads the selected description and notes.
Server-side code combines that content with the task instructions and sends the model request. It keeps the provider credential out of the browser.
The application checks the response's structure and any business rules it can enforce automatically.
The interface displays a labelled draft beside the source material for review.
The coordinator edits and accepts the summary through the application's normal controls.

Keep the task instructions specific. Tell the model to summarize the reported issue, preserve uncertainty, identify missing information, and avoid assigning staff or inventing a diagnosis. Provide source identifiers with the notes when the draft needs to refer back to them.
For example, the portal receives:
Request description:
Water collects beneath the kitchen sink after use.
Note N1:
Resident says it happened twice this week.
Note N2:
No photo supplied. Nobody has inspected it yet.
The desired draft could read:
Problem Summary:
Resident reports water beneath the kitchen sink after use, with two occurrences this week. The cause remains unconfirmed because no inspection has taken place.
Missing Information:
Photo of the affected area and confirmation of where the water appears.
Sources:
Request description, N1, N2.
A draft that identifies a broken pipe or promises an appointment would exceed the supplied information.
If the interface expects separate summary, missing-information, and source fields, define that response structure. Some providers offer schema-constrained output, as described in Anthropic's
structured-output documentation
. A correctly formatted response still needs factual and business checks. A valid source identifier alone does not prove that the source supports a statement.

Choose the simplest connection that fits the product. An existing backend may handle the request directly. Background processing may suit work that should continue after the user leaves the screen. A shared integration component may help when several features need the same controls. A framework or gateway needs a specific purpose before it becomes part of the architecture.
Also distinguish
calling a model API
from
letting the model request actions through your business APIs

. Generating a summary requires the former. Letting the model propose an appointment or update a record adds action permissions and validation decisions. Keep those actions outside this example's first release.
Step 5: Handle Incorrect Answers, Delays, and Failures

Design the unsuccessful paths alongside the successful one. A fluent summary can omit a crucial note or state an assumption as a fact. A model request can also fail or take longer than the coordinator can reasonably wait.
Keep the original request visible and make the generated status clear. The portal should let the coordinator edit or discard the draft without changing the source notes.
Agree the behavior for each important case:
Case
Portal Behavior
Missing details
Identify what is unknown without filling the gap
Invalid response
Show a clear failure state instead of a broken draft
Slow request
Let staff continue working and explain the request status
Provider failure
Preserve the manual summary path
Record changed
Flag that the source changed before staff accept an older draft
Set a timeout and define whether a failed request may retry. Limit retries so one user action cannot create uncontrolled repeated calls.
Treat descriptions, documents, and notes as untrusted content. Someone could place instructions inside a note that attempt to redirect the model. OWASP's
prompt-injection guidance
describes this risk and recommends layered controls, including restricted privileges, output validation, and human approval for sensitive actions. Prompt wording alone cannot guarantee protection.
Step 6: Test the Feature and Plan a Limited Release

Test the application behavior and the generated content as separate concerns. A feature can pass its permission checks while producing poor summaries, or produce good summaries while exposing records to the wrong user. Both need review before release.

Build a permitted sample set that reflects the work staff actually encounter. Include short and long requests, missing details, contradictory notes, later corrections, and text that tries to override the task instructions. Keep expected behaviors with the examples so reviewers know what they are checking.
Use the portal's requirements to connect tests with responsibilities:
Requirement
Expected Behavior
Review Check
Reviewer
Preserve meaning
Draft keeps the reported issue and uncertainty
Compare draft with source notes
Coordinator
Respect access
Users receive only permitted content
Test roles and record boundaries
Developer
Survive failure
Manual handover remains available
Simulate timeout and provider error
Developer
Avoid hidden changes
Drafting does not assign staff or change status
Inspect records before and after
Developer
Help the task
Review effort makes the draft worthwhile
Compare the full handover process
Product owner and staff

Agree what would prevent release, what staff may correct during a limited trial, and who decides whether the feature is useful enough to continue. Choose response-time expectations and quality criteria around the actual task.

Release to a small agreed group first. Record generation failures, response times, usage, and staff corrections using the data handling rules from Step 3. Give the owner a way to disable generation while keeping the ordinary workflow available.
Repeat the relevant quality checks when the prompt, model, or source-data path changes. Save enough version information to connect a reported problem with the configuration that produced it.
Step 7: Budget for Building and Operating the Feature

Estimate the work around the model call as well as the call itself. Existing-system integration can require interface changes, permission checks, data preparation, response validation, testing, and support. The application's condition affects how much work each part needs.
Separate the initial build from ongoing operation:
Cost Area
Questions Behind the Estimate
Application changes
Which screens, server components, and deployment steps change?
Data preparation
Can the application already retrieve permitted, usable input?
Quality checks
Who prepares examples and reviews generated results?
Model usage
How many requests, how much input, and how much output?
Operation
Who handles hosting, failures, updates, and support?
Staff review
How much checking and correction does each draft require?

Model providers often measure usage in tokens, which are units of input and output content. Longer notes, longer responses, repeated attempts, and more frequent use can change the usage bill. Check the chosen provider's current pricing and your expected workload before estimating that bill.

For the portal, count expected handovers and examine representative note lengths. Include failed attempts and retries in the assumptions. Set usage limits or alerts appropriate to the account and application.
Step 8: Clarify Responsibilities Before Development Starts

Agree who supplies the inputs, makes business decisions, and owns the feature after release. One person may hold several roles, but the project still needs a clear answer when access, feedback, payment, or support becomes necessary.
Use the following allocation as a discussion starter. Your actual engagement should name the responsible people and state which work the estimate includes.
Responsibility
Agreement to Record
Application access
Who provides access and answers questions about the existing system
Example data
Who supplies permitted records and explains their meaning
Scope and rules
Who approves the task, exclusions, and access boundaries
Implementation
Who builds, tests, and documents the integration
Review and release
Who checks usefulness and authorizes the limited release
Accounts and support
Who owns credentials, pays usage charges, and handles changes
Keep these agreements with the task definition from Step 1 and the release checks from Step 6. Record unresolved dependencies, who will investigate them, and which decisions must wait for an answer.
Final Thoughts

If you want me to assess an LLM feature for your existing application, describe the product, the task staff perform today, and the result you want to improve. Include the available data and any known access constraints so we can identify what needs investigation before defining the work.
Frequently Asked Questions
These answers address missing application interfaces, the need for company documents, and the effort required to review generated content. Use them to resolve questions about your proposed feature.
What If Our Application Has No Suitable API or Documentation?
A developer can check for a backend change, connector, or permitted export. The available route depends on your access, application restrictions, and how current the data must be.
Does the Feature Need Our Company Documents or Model Training?
Not necessarily. A summary may need only the request and notes. Questions about company procedures need relevant documents, which the application can supply or retrieve without training the model.
Could Reviewing AI Output Take More Time Than the Feature Saves?
Yes. Compare time spent reviewing and correcting drafts with the manual process. Developers also raise
concerns about hidden errors and rework
. Revise or stop the feature if the extra checking outweighs its usefulness.
